item.title: Australia's ancient rainfall patterns more complex than previously believed
item.description: "Sediment and fossil records are a major pillar of our understanding of how the climate works—but climate scientists have gotten something wrong about Australia's ice age," says Dr. Alex F. Wall, lead author of a new research paper published in Quaternary Science Reviews. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Invisible work' of AI falls disproportionately to middle managers, women
item.description: It's a common refrain that AI is changing how we work, but new research conducted by the Notre Dame-IBM Tech Ethics Lab, housed in the Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, shows that AI is creating new forms of work and reconfiguring employees' lived experience of work itself. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Weeping whales: Stillborn humpback whale grieving documented
item.description: Humpback whale mothers may experience grief when their calves die, a rare research observation led by Griffith University and Sea World Foundation has found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nine in 10 UK gambling websites breach data privacy law, study finds
item.description: Nearly nine in 10 (86%) UK-licensed online gambling websites are operating in breach of the General Data Protection Regulation, according to new research from the Gambling Research, Education and Treatment (GREAT) Center at Swansea University published in the journal Computers in Human Behavior Reports. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: En los acantilados de Asturias han encontrado un animal que hasta ahora solo conocíamos de Reino Unido
item.description: En 2009, José Antonio Sánchez Féliz, vecino de Madrid, paseaba por los acantilados de la playa de Vega, en Ribadesella, cuando tropezó con unos huesos oscuros clavados en la roca. No imaginó que acababa de tocar un ictiosaurio de 192 millones de años. Tampoco que su hallazgo tardaría 17 años en confirmar algo que la ciencia europea nunca había visto fuera de Reino Unido. Seis expertos, tres países, un solo animal . El anuncio llegó desde el Museo del Jurásico de Asturias . Investigadores de Argentina, Estados Unidos y España compararon los huesos con cientos de ejemplares británicos y… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Isra Fdez

item.title: Forget robots: Scientists turn cockroaches into cyborg first responders that could save lives
item.description: Innovative researchers have engineered cyborg cockroaches designed for use in disaster rescue missions. These remarkable insects possess the ability to locate victims and deliver crucial medical assistance. Outfitted with cameras and injection systems, they skillfully maneuver through debris. This cutting-edge advancement aims to elevate search and rescue efficiency in tough terrains, with hopes for real-world implementation during future emergencies. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: First-of-its-kind preventive phage therapy provides promising results against Salmonella
item.description: The mammalian gut microbiome teems with a delicate balance of bacteria and the viruses that keep them in check, called bacteriophages, or phages. Each bacterial species usually has its own set of phage partners. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New simulations link unusual particle diffusion to yielding in soft jammed matter
item.description: Soft materials such as colloidal suspensions, emulsions, foams and gels often display complex and unusual behaviors compared with ordinary solids or liquids. From a mechanical point of view, for instance, they can resist deformation like solids, but they can also start to flow like liquids when a sufficiently strong external drive is applied. This transition from solid-like to liquid-like behavior, known as "yielding," is central to the physics of soft amorphous materials and to many industrial and biological processes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Born-again' star offers rare chance to watch stellar evolution in real time
item.description: Astronomers have confirmed that one of the fastest-changing stars ever observed has entered a new stage of its evolution, offering a rare opportunity to watch a star's life unfold on human timescales. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Speeding glaciers drive half a century of polar ice loss
item.description: The longest satellite record ever assembled shows that Greenland and Antarctica have lost 11.3 trillion metric tons of ice since the 1970s, raising global sea level by more than 3 centimeters (1.2 inches)—and that most of the loss has come from glaciers flowing faster into the ocean, not from melting at the surface. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The local costs of remote sensing: Examining the ethics of laser scanning in tropical forests
item.description: Laser scanning, often referred to as lidar, has rapidly transformed how tropical forest regions are studied, monitored and understood across academic disciplines. The technology enables researchers to peer through dense forest canopies, rapidly providing high-resolution scans of the landscape below. This growing observational power is central to the scientific value of remote sensing technologies but also brings into focus the conditions, interests and power structures under which they are used. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Purple swirls on the Red Planet
item.description: This image shows a prominent ice cliff near Mars’s south pole. With striking swirls of purple, pink and red, it’s a far cry from the colour palette we usually associate with the Red Planet. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: SpaceX prepares for first orbital flight of Starship rocket
item.description: SpaceX announced Tuesday that it was planning to send its flagship rocket, Starship, into orbit, a key step in its project to one day reach the moon or Mars. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US acknowledges for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space
item.description: The United States has confirmed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space, a remarkable revelation after previous warnings about countries such as Russia possibly weaponizing a global frontier long agreed in treaties to be used for only peaceful purposes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Well-preserved tooth from Pacific mastodon found in a creek in San Francisco Bay Area
item.description: Brigid Lynch was working along a wooded creek in a mountainous part of the San Francisco Bay Area when something that didn't look like the rocks she'd been studying caught her eye. It turned out to be the fossilized tooth of a Pacific mastodon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Should Beijing use its maritime militia as a backup force in the South China Sea?
item.description: China should strengthen its maritime militia to be an extra force to collect information and maintain a regular presence in the South China Sea, where it is coming into frequent conflict with the Philippines. That was the suggestion Wu Shicun, the founding president of China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies, made on Tuesday on the sidelines of the Beijing Xiangshan Forum, an annual defence gathering in the capital attended by security officials and researchers from nearly 100... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Amber Wang,Albee Zhang

item.title: A world 20 light-years away reveals surprisingly organized, Jupiter-like weather
item.description: Scientists from Trinity College Dublin have developed a way to unravel changing weather patterns on distant worlds. Using this approach, they discovered that the weather on a well-studied brown dwarf, SIMP 0136, previously linked to northern lights-like phenomena, is largely shaped by just two dominant processes: changes in temperature and the vertical structure of its clouds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study finds violence affects millions across US with links to health, economic hardship
item.description: A new national study reveals the widespread reach of violence across the United States, finding that more than half of U.S. adults have experienced physical violence and nearly half have experienced sexual violence in their lifetimes. The U.S. National Study on Violence Experiences Across the Lifespan (USVEX) also shows stark disparities in who experiences violence and how closely violence is linked to economic hardship, mental health and substance use. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Students in Gaza ‘devastated’ after plan for them to study in Belgium fails
item.description: Belgian government unable to agree on evacuation of 13 students to take up scholarships at universities Students who are unable to leave Gaza and take up scholarships at Belgian universities have said they are devastated after Belgium’s government hit deadlock on a plan enabling them to leave the war-torn territory. Ahmed Abujami, a 28-year-old doctor in Gaza, said he was “deeply disappointed” after Belgium’s five-party coalition government last Friday failed to agree on an evacuation plan for 13 students and researchers in the territory. Abujami has a scholarship to do a one-year master’s… Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels

item.title: Chinese scientists build world’s smallest CT scanner, weighing just 6kg
item.description: Chinese researchers have developed the world’s smallest CT scanner, a portable device designed to produce images of tiny fossils and archaeological relics. Built by the Shandong province-based Rayim, the Xtomo-Cube is about the size of a desktop speaker and weighs just 6kg (13.2lbs). “The device can be held in one hand and is the world’s smallest and lightest CT system, earning it the nickname ‘palm-sized CT scanner’,” Liu Baodong, a senior engineer at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and general... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.title: Chimpanzees give youngsters the tools to learn tricky techniques
item.description: Two-thirds of a century after Jane Goodall observed "David Greybeard" break off a twig to fashion a fishing rod for termites, researchers following in her footsteps have found that adult chimpanzees in Senegal literally hand youngsters the tools for learning. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Transparency and trust are the foundations of every successful research partnership, report suggests
item.description: According to research by the IfM Bonn, strengthening research collaboration between universities and businesses requires regional technology transfer networks in which technology transfer offices at universities and research institutions, as well as chambers of commerce and industry, trade associations, chambers of crafts, business-related networks and financial intermediaries, all play an active role. In this way, networking opportunities could be pooled and examples of good practice highlighted. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How high turnover rates in Tanzania's agro-dealer sector affect farmer fertilizer adoption
item.description: Smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa adopt agricultural inputs, including fertilizer, at low rates, contributing to low agricultural productivity. Previous research has shown that insufficient information and distrust in the quality of products for sale in local markets are among the reasons for low rates of fertilizer adoption and application. In a new study published in the American Journal of Agricultural Economics, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign researchers examined the agricultural marketplace in Tanzania, finding that frequent turnover among local agro-dealers affects… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new mechanism for reading extra-long genes in neurons
item.description: Neurons in humans and other mammals express many exceptionally long genes, ranging from more than 100 kbp to more than 2 Mbp, that are important for forming synapses and neural circuits. In general, genetic information is read from DNA into RNA. This process is called transcription. The longer a gene is, the more time it takes to read from beginning to end. In addition, gene expression must be regulated at several steps. Neurons are therefore thought to require special mechanisms to read long genes accurately and stably, but the details of these mechanisms have remained unclear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study explores new photonics advance: Topology imprinting in nonlinear metasurfaces
item.description: Light is traditionally described by properties such as wavelength, amplitude, phase and polarization. Advances in optics have shown that light can also be shaped into complex spatial patterns known as structured light, enabling new ways to carry information and interact with matter for applications in imaging, optical communications and information processing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reversed biological age in older adults in just 4 weeks
item.description: Older adults who changed the balance of fat, carbohydrates, and animal protein in their diets showed signs of reduced biological age after just four weeks. The strongest result appeared in participants eating an omnivorous, lower-fat, higher-carbohydrate diet. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Four in 10 young people don't see 'buy now, pay later' as debt
item.description: The way a product is labeled can change how consumers think about it. "No added sugar" or "99% fat-free" can make food sound healthier than it really is. Fuente: Phys.org.

Beijing is hosting China’s most important annual defence conference, the Beijing Xiangshan Forum, bringing defence officials, former politicians and think tank experts to the city from around the world. About 200 specialists and researchers are expected to take part in the forum this week, which many see as Beijing’s answer to Singapore’s annual Shangri-la Dialogue, the region’s biggest... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Greyhound racing just turned 100, and says its dogs are fine. But are they?
item.description: This year, greyhound racing in Britain turns 100 years old. The first race took place on July 24, 1926, in Manchester, where six dogs chased a mechanical hare around a track. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 16 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02914-6 Researchers detect more than 1,000 overlooked microproteins in human brain tissue, including some that are altered in Alzheimer’s disease. Fuente: Nature.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 16 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02886-7 An era-defining mathematics claim raises questions over how AI tools credit earlier work. Fuente: Nature.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 16 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02849-y Researchers are racing to culture a menagerie of exotic organisms and finding lots of surprises along the way. Fuente: Nature.

item.description: Estados Unidos confirmó por primera vez que desplegó armas en el espacio. El reconocimiento, emitido por el secretario de la Fuerza Aérea estadounidense, Troy Meink, generó controversia sobre la existencia de capacidades ofensivas y defensivas ubicadas en órbita, mientras aumentan las preocupaciones de Washington por las capacidades espaciales de Rusia y China. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: High-resolution weather data could pinpoint neighborhoods facing greatest heat stress
item.description: Heat stress is a leading cause of weather-related deaths and can be especially dangerous in cities, where phenomena like urban heat islands drive temperatures higher than in surrounding rural areas. Now, a new dataset developed by the U.S. National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) aims to provide city governments and health officials with information that could minimize heat impacts on residents. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New species of 240-million-year-old prehistoric animal could reshape dinosaur origins timeline
item.description: A new prehistoric animal species from Tanzania dating to around 240 million years ago, during the Triassic period, has been described by an international team of researchers. Led by the University of Bristol, the new species, named Dinodontosaurus isiyavamanda, could help scientists refine the age of one of the world's most significant fossil sites and reshape the timeline of early dinosaur evolution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plasma and electricity convert CO₂ into methanol, butane and other useful chemicals
item.description: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) can be harmful to the environment in large amounts but can be used in the production of fuels and other useful chemicals. Doing so isn't easy, though. Now, Yale researchers have developed a new way to combine electrocatalysis and plasma to efficiently and practically generate a number of valuable products from the gas. The results are published in Nature Catalysis. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Weather forecasts are significantly less accurate in poorer countries, analysis finds
item.description: Weather forecasts inform countless everyday decisions—from farmers deciding when to sow crops and energy companies anticipating demand to public authorities preparing for heat waves. But how useful those forecasts are depends considerably on where people live. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Young, eco-anxious Canadians are the most likely to support disruptive tactics by environmental activists, study finds
item.description: The tolerance of individual Canadians for radical forms of environmental activism depends on several factors. Overall, however, Canadians do not support vandalism or violence as forms of protest. Those are the key findings of a new study by researchers from McGill University and Université Laval. The findings are published in the Canadian Journal of Political Science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: History is being rewritten at an archaeological site in Morocco. What the discovery of an ancient wall tells us
item.description: In the hills of northwestern Morocco, overlooking the river that gives the site its name, research at Oued Beht is bringing to light a previously unknown chapter of the region's past. The discovery of a substantial built structure suggests that, during the second millennium BC, communities in northwestern Africa were actively shaping their environment. They were also engaging in broader networks of interaction across the Mediterranean world. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tracking the path of new world screwworm
item.description: New cases of New World screwworm have recently surfaced in the United States, highlighting the critical need to track its paths to determine where future infestations may occur. Researchers at the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Agricultural Research Service (ARS) are employing predictive models as part of a forward-thinking approach to manage New World screwworm. This strategy allows USDA agencies to act earlier, respond faster and direct resources where they are most needed to protect U.S. livestock, pets and wildlife. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What are best options for controlling GSL dust, and what would they cost?
item.description: A new collaborative report from University of Utah researchers and coordinated by the Wilkes Center for Climate Science & Policy provides Utah Department of Natural Resources, Department of Environmental Quality and policymakers with a comprehensive analysis of the growing risks posed by dust from the exposed lakebed of Great Salt Lake, the potential costs of controlling that dust, and the long-term benefits of stabilizing lake levels. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Webb reveals dynamic panorama of star formation, including smallest known brown dwarfs
item.description: This starry view of the nearby star-forming region IC 348 is one of the largest images released to date from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope. Using Webb, astronomers searched IC 348 for brown dwarfs, which are less massive than the smallest stars. The researchers discovered brown dwarfs just twice the mass of Jupiter, bringing the study of these curious objects into a new mass range and revealing new insights about the star-formation process. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Disordered atoms steer shared light pulses by matching motion and timing
item.description: A research team at the Institute of Applied Physics at TU Darmstadt has shown for the first time that atoms that are completely disordered and in constant motion can nevertheless emit jointly directed light preferentially in one direction—even though neither the atoms nor their environment exhibit a direction—and that the strength of this asymmetry can be specifically adjusted. The paper is published in the journal Physical Review Letters. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Skipping showers is the latest trend. But is there any science to 'pheromone' maxxing?
item.description: Across parts of the internet where young men trade tips on self-improvement, the latest project is scent. Deodorant is out, and washing less is in. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why most rivers don't respond to storms the same way twice
item.description: The same amount of rain falling on the same landscape at different times can send very different amounts of water into its rivers, according to a new study in Nature Water. The research offers a global picture of how catchments behave—not where rivers are or how much water they carry, but how consistently landscapes turn rainfall into river flow. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Exclusive: Alzheimer’s blood tests should not be used on their own and risk leading people to believe they are inevitably going to develop dementia
item.description: Exclusive: Alzheimer’s blood tests should not be used on their own and risk leading people to believe they are inevitably going to develop dementia THEGUARDIAN.COM Researchers warn social media driving harmful misuse of Alzheimer’s blood tests Fuente: The Guardian.

item.title: Smart nanoparticles deliver antibiotics directly to H. pylori
item.description: Helicobacter pylori bacteria infect around half the global population and are a leading cause of stomach ulcers and gastric cancer. While antibiotics remain the standard treatment, they often fail to reach bacteria hidden beneath the stomach's protective mucus layer and deep within ulcer tissue. This often requires higher antibiotic doses, increasing the risk of adverse effects and antibiotic resistance. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Adaptive crystal can selectively capture CO₂ and recognize similar molecules
item.description: Chemical separation can be energy-intensive when molecules have similar sizes and properties. Researchers from Shibaura Institute of Technology, Japan, have now developed an interlayer adaptive crystal that changes its spacing to recognize specific molecules. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Magnets could help quantum computers talk to each other, says researcher
item.description: Xufeng Zhang is using magnets to make computers more power efficient at the quantum level. The Northeastern professor of electrical and computer engineering recently published two papers highlighting small-scale magnetic systems he and his team developed that could help make computers much more power efficient in the future. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Home advantage or pastures new? High-Arctic shorebirds rarely return to the same breeding area
item.description: Shorebirds are capable of some of the longest migrations on Earth, yet most return year after year to the same area to breed. Coming back has distinct advantages, including knowing the best spots to feed or roost, having information about where predators lurk, and—hopefully—finding last year's partner again. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Great Salt Lake's ancient past reveals how quickly fresh water can disappear
item.description: From a mountainside overlooking Utah's Great Salt Lake, a time traveler turning back the clock 20,000 years would watch a dramatic transformation of the landscape. The shallow, salty lake below would swell into an immense body of fresh water, at one point reaching nearly 1,000 feet (305 meters) deep and covering more than 10 times the lake's modern area. Mountain ranges would become islands, and the new shoreline would move far beyond its current boundary. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New peanut genome map uncovers hidden gene, boosts dense-planting yields 20%
item.description: An international team that includes researchers from Murdoch University's Centre for Crop and Food Innovation (CCFI) has built the most comprehensive genetic map of the peanut yet and used this new genomic resource to breed a higher-yielding dwarf peanut line. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In Australia's most incarcerated place, most inmates have a mental illness
item.description: A new landmark study finds nearly two-thirds of NT prisoners have a diagnosed mental illness. Calls are now growing for more specialised services to reduce reoffending. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Tahnee Jash

item.title: Not all roads lead to Rome: Research challenges what we think we know about Roman roads
item.description: A multidisciplinary team of researchers from Aarhus University in Denmark, Queen Mary University of London and other European institutions analyzed a data set representing almost 300,000 kilometers (186,000 miles) of Roman roads across the former empire, creating the most detailed quantitative picture yet of how the Roman road network was structured. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Invites Media to International Observe the Moon Night
item.description: NASA will host an International Observe the Moon Night celebration from 5:30 to 8 p.m. CST on Saturday, Sept. 19, at the U.S. Space & Rocket Center, the official visitor center for NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. International Observe the Moon Night celebrates the Moon, the science behind it, and its connection […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Lee Mohon

item.title: Mitotic chromosomes may assemble from pre-existing chromatin 'building blocks' during cell division
item.description: Inside each human cell, about 2 meters (6.6 feet) of genomic DNA must be accurately copied and equally transmitted to two daughter cells during cell division. To achieve this, the copied DNA is condensed into thick, short structures called mitotic chromosomes. However, how chromatin is organized and condensed to form mitotic chromosomes has long remained a major question in genetics and cell biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Is science journalism dying? Comparing a 'science crash' 40 years ago to today
item.description: When two popular science magazines—out of about 17 in circulation—ceased publication in the same year, one commentator said, "The science magazines didn't shake out. They fell apart." The general manager of one of the failed magazines said, "There was a perception that they were irrelevant." One of the publishers remembered being in a "state of shock" as the failures emerged. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Record-breaking levels of plastic found in seabirds, with almost 900 pieces found in one bird alone
item.description: For more than a decade, it was thought that the world's most plastic-polluted birds couldn't get any more contaminated by the man-made material. But then, from 2023–2026, the record was broken every single year. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3D food printing of balanced vegetarian dishes from rice and lentil flours
item.description: Rice and lentils are a pairing that goes a long way back, whether as khichdi in India or mujaddara in the Middle East. On its own, each is a source of incomplete protein, short on certain essential amino acids—but paired together, they fill each other's gaps, and lentils also blunt white rice's high glycemic index. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Greenhouse gas benefits of agricultural irrigation far outweigh emissions costs, study finds
item.description: Irrigating U.S. crops prevents higher greenhouse gas emissions by avoiding land conversion, new research by Colorado State University shows. Agricultural irrigation allows the United States to grow more food on less land. If irrigation were suddenly shut off, the land-use change required to make up for lost yields would produce significantly more greenhouse gas emissions than irrigation emits—363 times more. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Meet Samuel Henderson, the 12-year-old who can mimic more than 100 bird calls and is now...
item.description: Samuel Henderson, a gifted young boy, has skyrocketed to social media fame with his extraordinary ability to mimic over one hundred bird species solely using his voice. His captivating talent has enchanted audiences worldwide, accumulating millions of views. Remarkably, wild birds often respond to his lifelike calls. Samuel now passionately advocates for wildlife conservation and encourages everyone to explore the great outdoors. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Necesitamos gasolineras espaciales para conquistar el cosmos. Un nuevo estudio cree que Titán podría ser una
item.description: Si queremos conquistar el espacio, necesitamos gasolineras espaciales. Construir naves más grandes, capaces de llevar una mayor carga de combustible, no es rentable. Esperar a que vengan naves de recarga puede suponer mucho tiempo y, también, un coste extra. Todo eso sin contar el consumo de recursos que supondría aquí en la Tierra. Por eso, hace tiempo que los científicos coquetean con la idea de buscar fuentes de combustible de las que se pueden obtener recursos directamente en el espacio. Hay varias candidatas; pero, según un estudio publicado hace pocos meses, la luna Titán podría ser una… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Heat-stable enzyme from deep-sea microbe turns nitrogen gas into ammonia
item.description: Microorganisms can do remarkable things—for example, nitrogen fixation, the conversion of nitrogen gas (N₂) into a form that organisms can use. Although nitrogen gas makes up around 78% of Earth's atmosphere, plants and animals cannot directly use it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How advertising turns our insecurities into profit—and how you can resist the manipulation
item.description: Have you ever bought something not because you wanted it, but because you were afraid of what might happen if you didn't? Maybe you worried about looking older, falling behind at work or simply not fitting in. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wild dogs make the longest recorded journey of any terrestrial mammal in Africa
item.description: African wild dogs (Lycaon pictus) travel incredibly long distances to search for a mate and new places to breed. They typically embark on these mammoth treks as young adults and often face numerous hazards along the way. These include busy highways, expanding human settlements and deadly wire poaching snares. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Avoiding a sticky situation: How cells stop messenger RNAs from clumping together
item.description: Messenger RNA, or mRNA, is best known for carrying genetic instructions from DNA to the cellular machinery that makes proteins. But all RNA molecules have another, less appreciated property: They are naturally sticky. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Frontline safety concerns mount among property managers, new survey shows
item.description: Safety and security challenges are creating unprecedented strain for frontline property management professionals, according to a new bilingual survey conducted by Portland State University's Center for Real Estate. Initiated after industry partners raised alarms about changing workplace conditions, the study offers insight into the daily risks experienced by property management staff at multifamily and commercial properties. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: CubeSat instrument extends solar storm warnings 10x
item.description: The sun is the reason life exists on our small, blue planet. It provides solar radiation that warms the planet and ignites intricate biochemical processes like photosynthesis, producing oxygen for life to breathe. However, while the sun is known for giving life, it can also take it away with solar flares, geomagnetic storms and solar radiation storms, collectively referred to as space weather. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Satellite data reveal ESG scores track public image more than actual forest loss
item.description: Environmental sustainability researchers at NUS found that widely used environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings often fail to reflect companies' actual exposure to deforestation, highlighting the need to integrate satellite-based environmental data into sustainable investing frameworks. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How individual cells 'surf' chemical waves to form a collective
item.description: Researchers have developed an innovative imaging technique to visualize the transition of single cells into multicellular organisms in new detail. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Biophysical model suggests how cells optimize information gathering without using too much energy
item.description: In both biological and engineered systems, cells and sensors must make sense of noisy, changing signals to function. However, collecting and using this information consumes valuable energy. A new study, published in Physical Review Letters, describes a model for how a sensor or cell might maximize information collection from its surroundings while controlling the overall energy cost, resulting in an optimized system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fertilizer study reveals where the world can boost food production and cut pollution
item.description: Global consumption of fertilizer has doubled since 1980, but some regions that have historically overused fertilizer, including China and parts of Europe, have taken steps to reduce use. Those are some of the findings of a new global dataset from the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research calls for more consistent, child-centered policing to build trust and protect children
item.description: New research co-led by the University of Bedfordshire and the University of Lancashire has highlighted the need for more consistent child-centered and safeguarding-led approaches across policing, with children and young people's experiences varying depending on where they live, whom they encounter, the reason for these encounters and how well systems support frontline practice. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Examining Americans' complicated relationship with science
item.description: A new study finds that while most Americans are interested in science and believe it benefits society, the public's relationship with science is more complicated than those positive views suggest. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: In April, the world watched as four humans circled the Moon for the first time in over 50 years with NASA’s Artemis II mission. On Saturday, Sept. 19, the public is invited to look up again with NASA events across the country, including the International Observe the Moon Night celebration held at NASA’s Goddard Space […] Fuente: NASA.

item.description: NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik (left) and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano view progress on the solid rocket booster integration in High Bay 3 inside the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. Bresnik, Parmitano, and NASA astronauts Andre Douglas, Frank Rubio, and Bob Hines made […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Planting trees in the wrong places is not a climate solution
item.description: A recent United Nations report has stated that the world will likely overshoot the 1.5°C target set out in the 2015 Paris Agreement by 2030. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Marine bacteria team up to break down one of the ocean's toughest carbon-storing molecules
item.description: Deep in the ocean, brown algae and diatoms produce a complex carbohydrate molecule called fucoidan, which helps form their protective outer layers. The fucoidan molecule is very difficult for microbes to break down because its chemical structure may include dozens of different linkages and branching patterns that vary from one algal species to another. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists create 'super ice' that is ten times stronger and far harder to shatter
item.description: Ice is cheap, abundant and surprisingly strong. But it has one major weakness: Cracks can race through it, causing it to shatter without warning. Now, scientists have developed a new material that could overcome that problem. Called BioPykrete, the reinforced ice is about 10 times stronger than ordinary ice and can absorb roughly 70 times more energy before breaking. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Advanced X-ray crystallography determines structure of macromolecule at unprecedented resolution
item.description: Proteins are high-performance molecular machines that carry out nearly every biochemical function inside living cells. To understand how they achieve this, scientists often examine their detailed atomic structure, which holds important clues to their activity. The more precision they achieve, the deeper the insight they may gain into the chemical principles that underlie protein structure and, ultimately, function. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient DNA traces medieval migration from Sweden to Finland
item.description: A new study led by the University of Turku provides new insights into the population history of Finland during the Late Iron Age and the Middle Ages. The researchers analyzed the genomes of people who lived in southwestern Finland and Häme between the 11th and 13th centuries to investigate how the population changed over the course of the Middle Ages and how people were connected to other regions around the Baltic Sea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Europe's e‑waste is a valuable resource—let's not throw it away
item.description: Throwing something away that is urgently needed, expensive and difficult to source sounds crazy. Yet of the 60 metals contained in old electronic devices such as phones, screens and washing machines, only a few are recycled. That includes precious metals such as gold and silver and other metals such as aluminum and copper. The rest are effectively single-use metals, used once and then lost during collection or through incineration. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists stunned as volcano cloud starts destroying methane
item.description: The Hunga Tonga eruption may have triggered a surprising chemical reaction that destroyed some of the methane released into the atmosphere. Scientists say the discovery could reshape estimates of methane pollution and inspire new methods for slowing near-term global warming. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Smelling chocolate helped men complete more reps without feeling more tired
item.description: Simply smelling chocolate helped men complete more leg extension repetitions without making the workout feel harder, with dark chocolate producing the strongest effect. The researchers think familiar food aromas may influence appetite and motivation by making the brain anticipate eating. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Han encontrado un planeta que no debería poder existir tan cerca de su estrella: es un mundo de agua que está condenado a morir
item.description: La búsqueda de los exoplanetas suele depender de un golpe de suerte, puesto que es necesario que el planeta pase exactamente por delante de su estrella desde nuestra perspectiva, bloqueando una fracción de su luz para que sea captado por nuestros telescopios. Sin embargo, el universo está lleno de mundos cuyas órbitas no se alinean con nuestros equipos, y ahora un equipo de astrónomos ha logrado detectar uno de estos "mundos invisibles" y sus características son extremas. Se ha publicado. A este nuevo hallazgo se le ha dado visibilidad gracias a un artículo publicado en la revista Astronomy &… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: José A. Lizana

item.title: Our new research shows humans have maligned bandicoots for decades, making them more vulnerable to extinction
item.description: Have you ever found your lawn riddled with holes or heard a little sneeze from your backyard bushes? Those are signs you might have a resident bandicoot. Bandicoots are nocturnal, rabbit-sized marsupials known for their pointy snouts, thin tails and large hind feet. Due to these features, they were originally misnamed after a type of rat from India, the pandi-kokku, or "pig-rat" (Bandicota sp.). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Laser altimeter BELA ready to explore Mercury's surface
item.description: Launched on Oct. 20, 2018, the joint ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission has traveled for almost eight years, using a carefully planned but eventful sequence of planetary flybys and solar-electric propulsion to gradually approach its destination, Mercury. The mission is now entering the final stage of its journey to the smallest and innermost planet of our solar system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: This Australian cave hid 25,000 years of ritual secrets
item.description: Microscopic plant remains are revealing how GunaiKurnai ancestors used Cloggs Cave for ritual practices over thousands of years. People deliberately gathered whole grasses, carried them into the dark cave, and burned them in thin layers, leaving behind traces that may span 25,000 years. A standing stone erected around 2,000 years ago and other ritual objects strengthen the evidence that the cave was a long-lived spiritual site. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A 5,000-year-old royal mystery: Digital clues point to Meretneith as Egypt's female king
item.description: More than 5,000 years ago, a royal woman named Meretneith (also written as Merneith) lived in ancient Egypt. She was possibly the daughter of Djer, the third king of the First Dynasty, a period when the first kings ruled over a unified Egypt. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a major brain shift between ages 50 and 75
item.description: Scientists have uncovered sweeping changes in how the human brain controls and organizes its genome beginning in midlife, offering new clues to why aging sharply increases the risk of Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases. One of the biggest shifts occurred between about ages 50 and 75, when many of the brain’s original immune cells declined and were replaced by cells with more inflammatory characteristics. Researchers also found weakening of cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier, along with widespread deterioration in the genome’s three-dimensional organization. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Children trust what they hear over what they see, study finds
item.description: New research from our Department of Psychology has revealed that children are far more likely than adults to judge a person's emotions by what they hear rather than what they see. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bubbles the food-stealing dolphin finds shortcut to easy meal
item.description: A dolphin that harasses fish until they regurgitate their food—then swoops in to steal it—has astonished University of the Sunshine Coast researchers who have documented this novel feeding strategy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: UV light reveals possible camouflage on a 125-million-year-old crocodile
item.description: A 125-million-year-old crocodile fossil has revealed preserved skin, possible sensory organs, sophisticated respiratory structures, and an unexpected pattern on its tail. Ultraviolet light exposed alternating bands that may represent ancient camouflage, potentially preserving the oldest known coloration in a crocodylomorph. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Invasive little fire ants prefer cooked beef, seeds over tuna
item.description: If you are trying to detect or bait little fire ants in your backyard, scientists at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa suggest swapping tuna for cooked beef and sunflower seeds. The study, published in the Journal of Applied Entomology by researchers at the UH Mānoa College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience (CTAHR), revealed that the little fire ant's (Wasmannia auropunctata) preferred diet is not what scientists and homeowners previously thought. In laboratory food-choice tests, the tiny, stinging pests overwhelmingly chose cooked beef and sunflower seeds over water-packed tuna. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Robots and AI uncover unexpected pathway in classic 135-year-old chemical reaction
item.description: Chemical reactions are often written as simple equations: Starting materials go in, and a product comes out. In reality, the same substrates can follow many different pathways depending on their concentrations, temperature, catalysts and other conditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Webb Reveals Dynamic Panorama of Star Formation
item.description: This starry view of the nearby star-forming region IC 348 is one of the largest images from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope released to the public so far. Using Webb, astronomers searched IC 348 for brown dwarfs, which are less massive than the smallest stars. The researchers discovered brown dwarfs just twice the mass of Jupiter, bringing the study of these curious objects into a new mass range. Publicado también por: European Space Agency. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Novel particle beam could challenge Einstein's theory of gravity
item.description: Does gravity act equally on all particles in the universe, or are there differences between ordinary and exotic matter? Physics professor Anna Soter and her team at ETH Zurich and the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen are investigating this question. "We have taken an important step toward carrying out an exciting experiment on this topic," says Soter. "We want to measure the gravitational interaction of the muon." Fuente: Phys.org.
